newsitem.title: USA: Cigarettes "habit forming", Philip Morris exec says.
newsitem.headline: Cigarettes "habit forming", Philip Morris exec says.

text.p: The head of the world's biggest cigarette maker testified in a landmark $5 billion secondhand smoking case Thursday that smoking could be "psychologically habit-forming" but was far from physically addictive.

James Morgan, chief executive of Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the biggest U.S. cigarette company, also testified in a videotaped deposition that he would not quit the tobacco business if cigarette smoking was proven to cause lung cancer and other diseases. He acknowledged that the great majority of people believe smoking causes cancer.

Morgan's testimony was taken April 14 in New York and shown late Thursday to jurors hearing the case brought on behalf of an estimated 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants suing tobacco companies for lung cancer and other diseases allegedly caused by cigarette smoke on airplane flights.

Excerpts of the deposition, including a portion in which Morgan described quitting smoking as similar to giving up Gummi Bears, jelly candy the executive himself eats regularly, were shown on television last spring.
Morgan said he smokes cigarettes and had quit three times since the late 1970s for various reasons and resumed smoking for the pleasure of it. "I did not find it difficult to quit," he said.

Under questioning from plaintiffs lawyer Stanley Rosenblatt, Morgan said cigarette smoking could not be called truly addictive since cigarettes neither intoxicated people nor required ever-increasing amounts to satisfy smokers.
But, he said, cigarette smoking was compelling and could be described as "behaviorly addictive" or "psychologically habit-forming."
The former head of the federal government's main cigarette-research group testified that secondhand cigarette on passenger jets was more dangerous than in the home.

"I would say the exposure in airplanes is much more intensive, much more serious, much more dangerous than the exposure in homes," said Ronald Davis, head of the U.S. Office of Smoking and Health from 1987 to 1991.
Davis told the six jurors that secondhand smoke contained up to 5,000 chemicals and was a health danger to anyone routinely breathing smoke from other people's cigarettes.
"It was definitely a cause of lung cancer in flight attendants who are exposed over a period of time to tobacco smoke," Davis said.
Smoking aboard U.S. airliners was banned in 1988. The seven tobacco companies and two industry groups fighting the lawsuit deny secondhand smoke caused the flight attendants' injuries.

Cigarette smoke contains lead, formaldehyde and benzene, among other cancer-causing agents, said Davis, a physician and expert in the causes of diseases. "Some of these elements are in higher concentration in the smoke that comes off the cigarette than the smoke the smoker takes in," Davis said.
He said modern aircraft were especially risky for secondhand-smoke exposure since dozens of passengers might be smoking and ventilation systems did not allow for fresh air.
"On an airplane, you can't open a window," Davis said.

The lawyers fighting the lawsuit say the average flight attendant spent only about 12 hours a week in closed aircraft cabins in the late 1980s and that the rate of lung cancer and other diseases among non-smoking flight attendants was the same as among other non-smokers.
The trial judge, Robert Kaye of Dade County Circuit Court, dismissed tobacco lawyers' complaints that he may have prejudiced the jury and refused to declare a mistrial.

Testimony in the case was to continue of Friday and was expected to last through at least September. It is both the first secondhand-smoke case and the first class-action lawsuit against the U.S. tobacco industry to come to trial. AMB.N
